summary: Defines URI fragment identifiers for text/plain content, letting links refer to a character range or line range. They can also carry integrity checks. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Normally a link points to a whole page. This lets a link say look at lines 10 to 12 of this text file.

subtitle: How a URL can point to a character range or a line range inside a plain text file.

tldr.problem: Links to a text/plain file can only point at the whole file, because plain text has no way to embed anchors the way HTML does.
tldr.mechanism: A fragment identifier such as #char=100 or #line=10,20 names a position or range counted in characters or lines, optionally followed by a length or MD5 integrity check.
tldr.outcome: Clients that implement it can jump to or highlight the referenced part, while clients that do not simply ignore the fragment and still retrieve the file. The RFC updates RFC 2046.

today: RFC 5147 is a Proposed Standard from April 2008 and updates RFC 2046. Neither the unit metadata nor the text records that it has been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Plain Text Needs Fragments
sections.content:
This memo updates the text/plain media type defined in RFC 2046 by defining URI fragment identifiers for it. A URI may end in a fragment identifier, separated by a number sign. The client interprets it after the file has been retrieved, so its meaning depends on the media type of the result. The best-known case is HTML, where a fragment names an element.

Plain text cannot hold invisible identifiers, so a fragment has to rely on properties the text already has: character positions and line positions. Being able to point at the part you care about saves readers the effort of searching for it.

Fragments are evaluated only by the client, after retrieval. A client that does not support them still retrieves the entity but cannot locate the part, which the RFC calls a reasonable fallback. A server has no reliable way to tell whether a client used a fragment.
sections.eli5: A plain text file has no signs or bookmarks inside it. So the link has to say how far to count: 'go 100 letters in' or 'go to line 10'.

sections.title: Positions, Ranges, Characters and Lines
sections.content:
Two ideas combine to give four kinds of fragment. A position is a point between characters or lines, a fragment of length zero, counted from zero. An entity with n characters has n+1 character positions. A range has a start and an end, and either can be left out to mean the beginning or end of the entity. The end must be greater than or equal to the start.

The ideas apply to characters and to lines. Line fragments include the line endings. An entity with no line endings is a single line.

Implementations MUST take the character encoding into account, because a character count and an octet count can differ. For example, UTF-16 uses two octets per character in most cases, and a leading byte-order mark does not count as a character.
sections.eli5: A position is the gap between two letters, like where a cursor blinks. A range is a stretch of letters between two gaps, like text you highlight.

sections.title: Fragment Syntax
sections.content:
The char and line schemes each take either a single number (a position) or two comma-separated numbers (a range). Keywords must be used exactly as given, in lower case. Examples of the forms are char=100, line=10,20, line=,1 (up to position 1) and line=10, (from position 10 to the end).

After the scheme, any number of integrity checks can follow, each introduced by a semicolon. A check is either length= with a number or md5= with 32 hexadecimal digits, optionally followed by a comma and a MIME charset name.
sections.eli5: The link is written like a short sentence: 'line equals 10 to 20', optionally followed by 'and the file should be this long' as a safety check.

sections.title: How Clients Process Fragments
sections.content:
Each line ending MUST be counted as one character, whether it is CR+LF, LF, CR or something else. Implementations MUST handle the conventions of the protocol and system they work with, SHOULD support the Internet-wide CR+LF convention, and MAY support others.

A position larger than the entity refers to the last position. A missing first value means the start, and a missing second value means the end. If a range's positions are not properly ordered, the fragment identifier MUST be ignored. A fragment with a syntax error MUST be ignored, and clients MUST NOT try to correct or guess it.

Integrity checks are optional for clients. If a client implements them and detects that the entity has changed, it SHOULD NOT interpret the fragment, and MAY tell the user. The length check is a very weak but easy check, and md5 is a fingerprint of 128 bits written as 32 hexadecimal digits. If a charset is given and differs from the entity's, the client MUST NOT use the check, though it MAY transcode first, which the RFC warns is unreliable. Unknown check types MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: If the link makes no sense, the program must ignore it and not guess. If the file seems to have changed since the link was made, it should not trust the line numbers.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four example URIs.

  • http://example.com/text.txt#char=100 is the position after the 100th character, or after the last character if the entity is shorter.
  • http://example.com/text.txt#line=10,20 identifies lines 11 to 20.
  • https://example.com/text.txt#line=,1 identifies the first line.
  • ftp://example.com/text.txt#line=10,20;length=9876,UTF-8 is lines 11 to 20, with a check that the entity is 9876 characters in UTF-8.

Protocols such as FTP give no explicit media type, so using fragments with them is inherently unreliable. Processing is only appropriate if the inferred type is text/plain.
sections.eli5: Because counting starts at zero, 'line 10 to 20' means the 11th through 20th lines. It is like counting the gaps between lines, not the lines themselves.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Software that supports these fragments behaves differently from software that does not, and different software may show fragments differently. That can mislead users, in ways similar to spoofing or phishing. The RFC's concern is mechanisms that show only the part of a document a fragment identifies, which could hide small-print legal text or include material that makes a fake site look real.

Suggested countermeasures include showing included content within clearly visible boundaries and limiting inclusion to the same security realm or to realms that give explicit permission. These issues apply on the client side, since fragments are not used when resolving a URI. Implementers should also read the security sections of RFC 3986 and RFC 3987.
sections.eli5: If a link shows only a slice of a page, someone could hide the important parts or make a fake page look real. Showing clear borders around the slice helps.

items.label: MD5 check
items.desc: 32 hexadecimal digits, optionally with a charset.
